idiom_name: sealed interface Op permits ... + records + switch with record patterns
implementation_notes: Java 17 sealed interfaces and records plus Java 21 pattern matching for switch make the classic Visitor structure unnecessary: `sealed interface Op permits Get, Put, Log {}` with one record per operation, and a single `switch (op) { case Get g -> ... }` expression that the compiler proves exhaustive - no default arm, and a new operation breaks every switch at compile time. Programs are immutable data (records), which is what makes equality-based tests and serialization straightforward. Keep the sealed form whenever the toolchain allows it; note that all permitted types must live in the same package/module, which is exactly the closed-set guarantee.
pitfalls: Sealed hierarchies must keep all implementations in one package (one module for named modules): splitting the algebra across modules defeats the check.
A `default` arm copied from pre-17 code silently restores the runtime failure the sealed switch just eliminated.
Records are shallowly immutable: a mutable array or collection field leaks mutability into 'data' programs and breaks equality-based expectations.

variants.name: Abstract Expression hierarchy + Visitor (Java 8)
variants.idiom_name: abstract class per operation + accept(Visitor) or interpret(Context)
variants.implementation_notes: On Java 8 the algebra is an abstract class with one subclass per operation; interpretation is either `interpret(Context)` on each node (a new operation edits every class) or a Visitor (`accept(v)` plus one visit method per node; a new operation is one new visitor). Programs are still values and testable without mocks, but equality must be hand-written and nothing checks that every operation was handled - the sealed-switch variant's guarantees are precisely what the newer language purchases. Choose this form only when the runtime floor is pinned below 17 or when the operation set must be extensible from other packages, which sealed types forbid.
pitfalls: The Visitor is the classic double-dispatch workaround: a missing override still compiles because interfaces are not checked for coverage, so tests/enumerations must cover the algebra.
Hand-written equals/hashCode on nodes is easy to get wrong and silently breaks data-based test assertions.
Adding a node type touches every visitor (or every node, for interpret-on-node); expect the algebra to be closed in practice.
